cross.h: Asia-Pacific plans lean toward governing and delivery
cross.t: In the 33 Asia-Pacific countries, Making Change Happen holds 26% of the latest national plan's responses, against 22% in the 14 comparator countries. The gap comes from delivery: agility and delivery capability is 8.8% against 6.9%, and authorised flexibility is 4.4% against 2.6%. Tackling structural exclusion goes the other way, at 3.0% against 5.9%, about half the comparator share.

cross.h: Climate is the region's storm, and ageing is rising up the list
cross.t: Climate change is tied to 16% of Asia-Pacific responses, against 11% in the comparators, and it leads in all four Asia-Pacific regions. The climate framework family holds only 5% of responses, so the risk is named more often than it is answered. Demographic shifts are tied to 4.9% of Asia-Pacific responses, against 2.8% in the comparators, and 11.6% in East Asia, the highest of any region.

cross.h: More urgent and a little more transformative than the comparators
cross.t: Asia-Pacific plans mark 23% of their responses as high urgency, about twice the comparators' 12%, with East Asia highest at 35%. Of the responses, 23% are transformative and 65% are business as usual, against 20% and 70% in the comparators. Those labels come from the national plans only. Sector plans, UNGA statements and budgets carry neither label.

cross.h: Asia-Pacific acts through organisations, rarely through money
cross.t: Nearly half of Asia-Pacific responses (47%) work through organisations: programmes, agencies and capacity. Only 6.8% use money such as grants, subsidies or tax measures, against 10.5% in the comparators. In the Pacific the figure is 3.9%, the lowest of any region, while Europe and Central Asia reaches 19%. Spending choices show up in budgets rather than in the plans, and the lever panel now ties the two where the match is clear.

cross.h: Asia leads on targets, but most responses still can't be tracked
cross.t: About a quarter of Asia-Pacific responses (26%) carry a quantified target, and 20% say how they will be monitored, against 23% and 16% in the comparators. South Asia (34%) and East Asia (32%) lead on targets. South-East Asia (19%) and the Pacific (21%) trail and sit closer to the Arab States and Latin America and the Caribbean (14% each). This holds back the RHDR Making Change Happen pillar across the region.

South-East Asia.h: Growth through clusters, skills and jobs, lighter on health
b: The region's plans favour linkages, clusters and cities (6.2% against 5.1%), knowledge (7.2% against 6.6%) and rapid resource mobilisation (3.9% against 3.1%). Jobs, places and mobility is above the average in 7 of 9 countries.
Health is light: long and healthy life is 4.2% against 5.1%, and only one country is above the average. Climate change is the risk named most, tied to 17% of responses.
Across seven countries' plan series, later plans put more on delivery capability (up about 1 point) and less on capabilities and domestic integration.

South Asia.h: The most specific plans, leaning to skills, trade and accountable government
b: South Asian plans are the easiest to place: 67% of responses reach a lever (63% on average), and 34% carry a quantified target (25% on average).
They lean to authorised flexibility (above the average in 7 of 9 countries), knowledge, reaching foreign markets and accountability. They put less on enterprise finance and on upgrading.
Across seven plan series, delivery capability is rising (up about 2 points) and domestic integration is falling (down about 3 points).

East Asia.h: Upgrading for export, under ageing and technology pressure
b: Export-led responses make up 13% of the latest plans (8% on average). Upgrading and innovation (9.3% against 5.1%) and linkages, clusters and cities are above the average in 4 of 5 countries. In plan series, export-led growth is rising (up about 5 points).

This is the only region where demographic shifts are among the top risks (12% of responses), alongside technological change (13%) and climate (14%). It also has the most responses marked high urgency (35% against 19%).
Enterprise finance is below the average in every country, and authorised flexibility is light. The five countries are China, Japan, Mongolia, South Korea and Taiwan.

Pacific.h: Plans for protection and stewardship, less for export growth
b: Future generations, the subpillar holding climate, natural capital and resilience, is 15% of responses against 13%. Climate is above the average in 7 of 10 countries.
Market rules and property rights stand out in all 10 countries, and economic and human wealth in 7. Land and resource tenure runs through Pacific plans.
Export-led growth is half the average (4% against 8%), upgrading and innovation is light (2.6% against 5.1%), and only 4% of responses use money as the instrument.

Europe and Central Asia.h: Competitiveness, connectivity and money on the table
b: Growth responses make up 43% of the latest plans, the highest of any region. Infrastructure and connectivity (7.6% against 4.4%, all three countries above the average), rural producers, reaching foreign markets and enterprise finance lead.
These plans use money more than any other region (19% of responses against 8%), and 70% of their responses reach a lever.
Three countries are read here: Kazakhstan, Poland and Serbia. Estonia's and Uzbekistan's documents yield too few responses to count.

Arab States.h: Resource stewardship and broad economic goals
b: Natural capital is twice the average (12.4% against 6.0%). Environmental degradation, resource pressures and climate are the leading risks (14 to 15% of responses each).
Enterprise finance (6.2% against 3.5%) and broad economic goals that fit no family (12%) are large, while governance is light.

This reads as Egypt's Vision 2030 alone. The documents for Morocco, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates yield too few responses to count, so treat this as a country note, not a regional message.

Africa.h: Living standards, trade and data, with fewer transformative responses
b: Decent standard of living (8.3% against 6.9%) and rural producers lean above the average. Reaching foreign markets (3.5% against 2.4%) and data sharing (2.3% against 1.1%) are above the average in 4 of 5 countries.
Natural capital (4.5% against 6.0%), climate and infrastructure are light. Fewer responses are framed as transformative than anywhere except the Arab States (17% against 22%).
Five countries are read here: Ethiopia, Ghana, Kenya, Nigeria and Rwanda. Their national plans and some budgets are in, but no sector plans or UNGA statements.

Latin America and the Caribbean.h: The most people-first plans, aimed at exclusion and places
b: People-first responses make up 49% of the latest plans, the highest of any region. Tackling structural exclusion is more than double the average (10% against 4%). Spaces, decent standard of living and markets are above the average in all five countries.
Infrastructure, authorised flexibility and enterprise finance are light.
The fewest responses are tied to a risk (28% against 37%), and the fewest carry a quantified target (14%). The five countries are Brazil, Colombia, Jamaica, Peru and Uruguay.
